Record date: 2129-12-30
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 12/30/29 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Continued shortness of breath, persistent cough with greenish sputum, and increased fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for follow-up five days post-admission for exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) complicated by pneumonia. He reports minimal improvement in his respiratory symptoms. The productive cough persists, yielding thick green sputum, and he continues to experience significant dyspnea, particularly at rest and with minimal exertion. The patient notes that he has been receiving nebulizer treatments every hour, but he feels they have provided limited relief.
Additionally, he reports that his fevers have been fluctuating, now averaging around 101F, and he experiences increasing fatigue that limits his ability to participate in daily activities. Mr. Fairfax expresses frustration with his slow recovery and worries about the potential for further deterioration of his lung function.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + increased fatigue, + intermittent fevers, - weight loss, - chills, + night sweats. Pulmonary - + persistent productive cough with greenish sputum, + increased wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 130/76 mmHg - Heart Rate: 92 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 28 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 85% on supplemental oxygen (4 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears fatigued and is in moderate respiratory distress, utilizing accessory muscles for breathing.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Severe wheezing on auscultation; decreased breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with prominent rhonchi; crackles audible throughout lung fields.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Extremities: No edema; no tenderness on palpation.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with persistent bacterial pneumonia, as evidenced by ongoing respiratory symptoms and hypoxemia despite aggressive management. 2. Persistent hypoxemia requiring close monitoring and potential escalation of respiratory support; patient remains at increased risk for respiratory failure. 3. Lack of clinical improvement in pneumonia symptoms; potential need for further intervention.
PLAN
1. Continue intravenous Levofloxacin 750 mg daily; reassess in 48 hours for clinical response and adjust based on culture results and sensitivities. 2. Perform repeat chest CT scan to assess for worsening pneumonia or development of pulmonary complications such as abscess or empyema. 3. Maintain supplemental oxygen at 4 L via nasal cannula; if oxygen saturation does not improve, consider escalation to non-invasive ventilation (NIV) support. 4. Increase oral Prednisone to 100 mg daily to further enhance anti-inflammatory effects; evaluate response in 48 hours. 5. Consult Infectious Disease for a comprehensive review of antibiotic regimen and consideration of alternative therapies based on clinical status and imaging findings. 6. Continue physical therapy interventions to promote respiratory function and physical conditioning as tolerated. 7. Monitor vital signs and respiratory status closely; prepare for transfer to the ICU if the patient exhibits any signs of clinical deterioration.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax remains hospitalized, with a continued focus on optimizing respiratory support and managing his COPD exacerbation and pneumonia. The treatment team will maintain vigilant monitoring of his clinical status and ensure timely interventions to mitigate complications. The patient is encouraged to voice any changes in his symptoms or concerns regarding his ongoing treatment plan.
